title: i-Ready Finally Has Real Research…And It Changes Nothing
author: The Digital Delusion
summary: The Digital Delusion reviews the first peer-reviewed study of i-Ready, published in Online Learning (Q1 journal), which examined two years of implementation across 131 Georgia schools and over 67,000 students. The study found effect sizes of +0.04 standard deviations in both reading and math—nearly identical to the previously available (but industry-funded and non-peer-reviewed) Johns Hopkins evaluations that had shown 0.8% improvement. The author praises the researchers for their candor about the observational design's limitations but critiques three methodological choices: converting 0.04 SD to 'two additional weeks of learning' without showing the calculation, underestimating program costs by calculating on active users (27,717) rather than all licensed students (67,602), and measuring outcomes on MAP Growth, which structurally resembles i-Ready's instructional format, raising questions about transfer. The article's central argument is that stronger evidence doesn't change the conclusion: i-Ready produces small effects at high cost, with many cheaper interventions (small-group instruction, after-school programs) likely generating better results for less money.
points: The strongest study ever conducted on i-Ready found effect sizes of +0.04 standard deviations in both reading and math—nearly identical to the previously available industry-funded evaluations dismissed by i-Ready advocates.

Converting 0.04 SD to 'two additional weeks of learning' is an inference not an observation: the calculation assumes learning accumulates at a constant rate throughout the year, an assumption neither defended nor justified in the paper.

The cost analysis dramatically underestimates i-Ready's expense by calculating subscriptions for 27,717 active users rather than the 67,602 students with access—potentially translating to $500,000-$1,000,000 spent per 0.01 standard deviation gained.

Measuring outcomes on MAP Growth—an adaptive computer assessment structurally similar to i-Ready's format—raises unresolved questions about whether effects would be smaller on less aligned assessments.
The study authors themselves note that other interventions (small-group instruction, after-school programs) almost certainly generate better results for far less cost.
quotes: That has finally changed. Last month, Online Learning – a Q1 educational journal – published the strongest evaluation of i-Ready to date.

'Our analyses are descriptive versus causal, as we cannot fully…understand or account for selection into treatment…[and] we were unable to account for other recovery interventions occurring during the same period.' That sentence gives me confidence in the paper: rather than overselling the findings, the authors openly acknowledge exactly what their design can (and cannot) tell us.
After two years, students who used i-Ready scored approximately: +0.04 standard deviations higher in Reading, +0.04 standard deviations higher in Math. That's it. That's the headline.
Ironically, the research so many people have been waiting for ultimately changes nothing: the evidence is stronger, but the conclusion remains the same.
The 'weeks of learning' reported in this paper is an inference, not an observed result. Accordingly, although it may make for an appealing headline, it is much less scientifically convincing.
Extrapolated, that suggests between $500,000 and $1 million dollars were spent for each 0.01 standard deviation growth amongst users: a substantially altered cost-benefit calculation.
